props.note: The composition is one the literature (lit. 1, 3, 5) says can be used for methanol synthesis; the basis of the percentages is not stated. No preparation, reduction, volume or space velocity of the design catalyst is given.

props.name: alkali side products
props.statement: Products of condensation and dehydration (esters, unsaturated hydrocarbons, ketones) form especially when the methanol-synthesis catalyst contains alkali metals.

props.name: ammonia methanol similar
props.statement: The pressure, temperature and heat of reaction of the synthetic preparation of ammonia and methanol are nearly equal, so many ammonia and methanol plants are built to run both processes.

props.name: basf 1923
props.note: history as the report gives it; the paragraph cites lit. 1 for the production and price figures
props.statement: Methanol production was first carried out on a large scale in 1923 by the Badische Anilin- und Soda Fabrik (B.A.S.F.), which also developed the catalytic synthesis of ammonia.

props.name: co conversion chosen

evidence.locator: p. 7, D. Keuze van het proces

props.statement: The CO conversion is in general the best process for methanol; hydrogen consumption and the purity of the crude methanol were decisive in this choice.

props.name: co2 process disadvantages
props.statement: The CO2 hydrogenation process is run under practically the same conditions as the CO process; its disadvantages are the purity of the crude methanol (by-products dimethyl ether, isopropyl alcohol, isobutyl alcohol, higher alcohols and esters; at most 75 % methanol) and a hydrogen consumption per methanol 1.5 times that of the CO process. It was first applied in the US by the Commercial Solvents Corporation (lit. 2).

props.name: cold gas temperature control

evidence.locator: p. 13, III Beschrijving van de procesgang
p. 13, III Beschrijving van de procesgang
p. 13, III Beschrijving van de procesgang

props.statement: Once the process has started, the reactor temperature is controlled by the amount of cold gas (25 °C) added between the catalyst beds, under each of the five upper beds; the total cold gas is controlled on the temperature of the gas leaving the reactor, kept constant at 350 °C.

props.name: dF reaction 1 highest
props.statement: The ΔF° of reaction (1), CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH, is higher than that of all the side reactions, so its equilibrium lies much less favourably.

props.name: equilibrium conversion 83
props.statement: If equilibrium is reached at 350 °C and 300 atm the CO conversion is 83.2 %.

props.name: industrial conditions
props.note: cited from lit. 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7
props.statement: In industry pressures of 250 to 350 atm, temperatures of 300 to 375 °C and space velocities of 30,000-50,000 are used (lit. 1, 3, 5, 6); very pure crude methanol (95-99 %) is obtained; with these high space velocities the CO conversion per pass is only about 12-16 % (lit. 2, 3, 7), far from equilibrium.

props.name: methanation most harmful
props.statement: Methane formation (CO + 3 H2 -> CH4 + H2O) is the most harmful side reaction: it is very strongly exothermic, more so than methanol formation, and can lead to hot spots; hot spots and the associated ruin of the catalyst must be prevented.

props.name: natta adsorbed phase h2 co ratio

evidence.note: read as 'a larger yield is obtained when in the synthesis gas c(H2)/c(CO) > 2'; quote withheld: sha256:3431244d6cd4477ab70195fb4f725b850257373e4964615ea75ba05182b31b39 chars:129

props.note: cited from Natta, 'Catalysis' vol. 3 (Emmett, ed., 1955) (lit. 3)
props.statement: With very selective catalysts a larger yield is obtained when the H2/CO ratio in the synthesis gas exceeds 2. Natta showed that the CO-H2 reaction is described quite well by a mechanism in the adsorbed phase, and that at large space velocities CO is adsorbed much faster than H2; so an H2/CO ratio above two must be applied in the gas to obtain the stoichiometric ratio of two in the adsorbed phase.

evidence.note: transcription withheld: sha256:46ec5c4cce4133308a97badaf79515f503db9de5a5d9d6c84ae83bf09617a280 chars:231; second_reading withheld: sha256:2717991a7114d347b4471fd501531c5dea0e98e1c0e7680e33dbccc795aa5869 chars:271

props.note: cited from Natta, 'Catalysis' vol. 3 (Emmett, ed., 1955) (lit. 3); rows read from the page image on 2026-09-29 (the text layer printed the columns apart from the reactions)
props.statement: Natta's table of the reactions of CO and H2 gives ΔH(350 °C) and ΔF°(350 °C) in kcal/kmol: (1) CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH -24450, +12100; (2) 2 CO -> CO2 + C -41430, -16730; (3) CO + 3 H2 -> CH4 + H2O -52222, -15826; (4) n CO + 2n H2 -> CnH2n + H2O not given; (5) 2 CH3OH -> CH3OCH3 + H2O -4600, -1400; (6) higher-alcohol and (7) acid formation not given; (8) CO2 + 3 H2 -> CH3OH + H2O -15335, +15800.

props.name: no iron nickel

evidence.note: '~zer' = ijzer (iron); '4000C' read as 400 °C; quote withheld: sha256:96ed2b43f5840a4edaa1a9db2db89550f8f84395080f58c14ee7589476525fe2 chars:134
'(c::::: 3700 C)' read as about 370 °C; quote withheld: sha256:fec3066e627aada6ae32cb1f40d2893234b0ed79bd6328e372d1bebd3d8020a6 chars:137

props.statement: The catalyst must contain no iron or nickel, which catalyze the conversion of CO to CH4, especially above 400 °C; at lower temperatures (about 370 °C) even traces are not ruinous. Very active iron or nickel can deposit on the catalyst by decomposition of Fe(CO)5 or Ni(CO)4, which must therefore not be present in the synthesis gas.

props.name: oil lowers activity
props.statement: Oil droplets are always carried along by the gas when it is compressed; the oil is adsorbed on the catalyst and strongly lowers its activity, so it must be removed from the synthesis gas.

props.name: pressure and inerts
props.statement: CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH proceeds with a large decrease in volume, so raising the total pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right; with inert gases such as N2 in the synthesis gas even higher pressures are needed, since the rate depends on the activities (proportional to the partial pressures) of CO and H2.

props.name: purge constant composition

evidence.locator: p. 13, III Beschrijving van de procesgang

props.statement: Part of the circulating gas is purged so that the composition of the gas to the reactor stays constant; otherwise the inert gases (N2, CH4) would accumulate and lower the yield.

props.name: selective catalyst needed
props.statement: Of the many possible reactions of CO and H2 the equilibrium of CO + 2 H2 -> CH3OH is the least favourable, so a very selective and active catalyst is needed and the usual hydrogenation catalysts cannot be used; the reaction is feasible only over a limited temperature range: below 300 °C the rate is too small and above 400 °C the equilibrium is very unfavourable.

props.name: selective catalysts found
props.note: cited from lit. 3 (Natta) and 5 (Groggins)
props.statement: It has proved possible (lit. 3, 5) to find catalysts that promote exclusively the reduction of CO to methanol while all other side reactions are almost completely suppressed, at least when the temperature does not exceed 390 °C.

props.name: stainless steel against co
props.statement: CO can react with the walls of the reactor, heat exchanger, condenser and pipes, and the iron carbonyl formed is very harmful to the activity of the catalyst; a thin copper or bronze lining is not always sufficient because it can melt at local very high temperatures, so modern plants make these of stainless steel (18 Cr-8 Ni).

props.name: synthesis gas raw materials

evidence.locator: p. 9, F. plaats van de fabriek

props.statement: CO and H2 can be made in many ways; the most important raw materials are water gas (steam over glowing coke at 1000 °C, or methane/natural gas with steam at 800 °C over a nickel catalyst; higher hydrocarbons and refinery off-gases can also be used), thermal cracking of hydrocarbons (hydrogen as a by-product of carbon-black manufacture) and CO as a by-product of calcium-carbide manufacture; the plant is best placed near ample coke or natural gas.
